questions.question: What is a sitemap primarily useful for?
options: Exposing an inventory of candidate URLs, including orphans with no inbound links
Certifying that every listed page passes the crawler's quality and spam filters
Overriding robots.txt for the paths the publisher chose to list inside it
Guaranteeing that every listed URL still resolves to fetchable content today

questions.question: What acquisition role do RSS and Atom feeds usually serve best?
options: Enumerating a publisher's complete archive, since feeds retain every past item
Discovering recent or updated items incrementally, using stable entry IDs
Confirming deletions, since an item leaving the window proves it was removed
Authorizing ingestion of linked content that robots.txt would otherwise block

questions.question: Yesterday's sitemap has 100,000 URLs and today's has 100,500, including 500 new URLs. What should happen to the new entries?
options: Fetch them ahead of robots.txt checks, since the publisher listed them itself
Record them as indexed documents, since the sitemap asserts they are canonical
Normalize them, apply scope policy, and enqueue the survivors as candidates
Retire the 100,000 older entries, since the newer file supersedes yesterday's

questions.question: Version 7 update arrives after version 8. How should the sink prevent regression?
options: Apply each event in arrival order, since queues deliver events at least once
Discard the stored version 8 first, then write version 7 as the live record
Merge both payloads into one record and let extraction resolve the conflict
Compare the source version and write only when it exceeds the stored version

questions.question: Why combine push notifications with periodic inventory reconciliation?
options: Push cuts detection lag while an inventory diff catches dropped or stale events
Reconciliation scans make idempotent writes and stable event IDs unnecessary
Push delivery is exactly-once and ordered, so the diff only measures latency
The two channels agree by construction on timestamps and deletion semantics

questions.question: What does an HTTP 304 response prove during a conditional sitemap fetch?
options: That every page listed inside the sitemap is unchanged since the last crawl
That the sitemap resource itself is unchanged under the validator you sent
That URLs absent from the previous fetch have been deleted by the publisher
That scope and robots checks may be skipped for URLs already seen once

questions.topic: Search APIs as an Acquisition Channel
questions.question: What should a search API result set be treated as?
options: A complete enumeration of the provider's index for the domains you queried
A publisher-authorized snapshot that carries permission to ingest the pages
A ranked sample of results the provider chose to return for that one query
A durable document store you can cite instead of fetching the source pages

questions.topic: Search APIs as an Acquisition Channel
questions.question: Why is cursor pagination often safer than offsets for changing results?
options: Cursors pin the provider's index so no result can change while you paginate
Cursors are exempt from request quotas, so deep pagination costs nothing
Offsets hold a stable snapshot by definition, so pages never shift mid-crawl
Opaque continuation state limits page drift when results are inserted later

questions.topic: Search APIs as an Acquisition Channel
questions.question: Three query variants each return 100 results but overlap heavily. What should be retained after URL deduplication?
options: The unique canonical URLs, plus the query, rank, and cursor that found each
Only the final query string, since earlier queries returned the same pages
All 300 result rows as distinct sources, since each came from its own query
Only the returned snippets, since the source URLs can be re-derived later

questions.topic: Search APIs as an Acquisition Channel
questions.question: Why should search snippets not normally become authoritative corpus text?
options: Snippets are assembled from the provider's cache, so they are always current
Snippets are query-biased fragments, incomplete, and sometimes out of date
Snippets contain no words from the source page, only a provider paraphrase
Snippets carry stronger rights metadata than a document fetched from its host

questions.topic: Search APIs as an Acquisition Channel
questions.question: Which metric best reveals diminishing value from a query family?
options: The provider's total result count, summed over every query before dedup
The mean rank at which in-scope results appear on the first returned page
New unique in-scope discoveries contributed per additional API request
The share of requests completing without a 429 or a transient provider error

questions.topic: Search APIs as an Acquisition Channel
questions.question: A provider returns HTTP 429. What is the correct response?
options: Rotate API credentials so the next call arrives under a fresh quota bucket
Raise request concurrency until enough calls slip past the rate limiter
Record the query as exhausted, since 429 means no further results remain
Honor the provider's retry guidance, back off, and stay inside the quota

questions.topic: Seed Selection and Crawl Scope Policy
questions.question: What is a crawl seed?
options: A starting resource from which link discovery and traversal begin
A URL held back until every other in-scope page has been fetched
A sampled page reserved for measuring ranking quality after indexing
A checkpoint record of every page fetched during one crawl session

questions.topic: Seed Selection and Crawl Scope Policy
questions.question: When should a discovered URL be checked against scope?
options: After extraction, once its content type and language can be measured
Before it enters the frontier, and again on each redirect target
Only when its response body exceeds the configured maximum size
After the whole host is crawled, during the corpus-level sweep

questions.topic: Seed Selection and Crawl Scope Policy
questions.question: Why is dropping every query parameter unsafe?
options: Parameters are the only place tracking IDs appear, so provenance is lost
Scope rules cannot be evaluated against a URL whose parameters were removed
Semantic parameters such as version select genuinely different resources
Stripping multiplies aliases, since each variant then hashes to its own key

questions.topic: Seed Selection and Crawl Scope Policy
questions.question: Why must redirect targets be scope-checked again?
options: A redirect always lands on the same host, so only its path needs rechecking
The redirect status code alone determines whether the target may be fetched
Approval of the source URL carries forward to whatever target it points at
An in-scope URL can redirect to an out-of-scope host or a private address

questions.topic: Seed Selection and Crawl Scope Policy
questions.question: How should a new seed's value be evaluated?
options: Crawl to a fixed budget and count the new in-scope canonical documents added
Count every URL the seed reaches, treating repeat discoveries as coverage
Prefer the seed whose homepage carries the most outbound navigation links
Compare raw fetch totals per seed, ignoring host, path, and date spread

questions.topic: Seed Selection and Crawl Scope Policy
questions.question: Why is broad crawling followed by deletion an unsafe scope strategy?
options: Deletion is irreversible, so a wrongly removed document cannot be recrawled
The fetch itself can breach policy and admit untrusted content to systems
Deleting rows after ingestion removes the request cost and rate-limit load
Scope rules can only be evaluated once extraction has produced clean text
